extract:
John Coltrane was an American jazz saxophonist and composer born on September 23, 1926, in Hamlet, North Carolina, and raised in High Point. After his mother moved north, he settled in Philadelphia, where he studied music and came up through the city's rhythm-and-blues and bebop scene. His recording career ran from the late 1940s until his death from liver cancer on July 17, 1967. In that relatively short span he moved from sideman in the bebop idiom to one of the most influential improvisers and bandleaders in jazz history.

Coltrane began on alto saxophone, inspired above all by Charlie Parker, and played in a Navy band in Hawaii in 1945–46. Back in Philadelphia he worked with Eddie "Cleanhead" Vinson, switched to tenor, and played in Dizzy Gillespie's band and later with Johnny Hodges. His breakthrough came in 1955 when Miles Davis hired him for the quintet with Red Garland, Paul Chambers, and Philly Joe Jones, recording for Prestige and Columbia. After being fired in 1957 over his heroin addiction, he got clean and spent a crucial stint with Thelonious Monk at the Five Spot. There he developed the dense, rapid-fire approach critic Ira Gitler called "sheets of sound."

The late 1950s were a prolific period of Prestige sessions, many engineered by Rudy Van Gelder and produced by Bob Weinstock. Blowing dates included Tenor Conclave with Hank Mobley, Al Cohn, and Zoot Sims; Interplay for 2 Trumpets and 2 Tenors; Wheelin' and Dealin'; and Cattin' with Coltrane and Quinichette alongside Paul Quinichette. He also appeared on Tommy Flanagan's The Cats and Mal Waldron-led sessions such as Mating Call, released under Tadd Dameron's name. His sole Blue Note album as leader, Blue Train (1957), with Lee Morgan, Curtis Fuller, and Kenny Drew, featured the title track and "Moment's Notice." He rejoined Davis for Milestones and Kind of Blue. Then he signed with Atlantic, where Giant Steps (1960) unveiled the cycling chord movement now called "Coltrane changes," heard on the title track and "Countdown," along with the ballad "Naima."

From 1960 he led the classic quartet with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones. With them he turned "My Favorite Things" into a soprano saxophone showcase. After moving to Impulse! under producer Bob Thiele, he recorded Live at the Village Vanguard with Eric Dolphy, Ballads, John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman (his vocal jazz landmark), Crescent, and the devotional suite A Love Supreme (1965). His late work, including Ascension and Meditations, embraced free jazz with Pharoah Sanders, Rashied Ali, and his wife Alice Coltrane on piano.

Critics were initially divided over his late experiments, and some dismissed them as "anti-jazz." Over time, however, A Love Supreme and Giant Steps became canonical, regularly ranked among the greatest jazz recordings ever made. Giant Steps remains a rite of passage for improvisers. His spiritual seriousness inspired the founding of the Saint John Coltrane African Orthodox Church in San Francisco. He received a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award and a Pulitzer Prize special citation in 2007.

His legacy continues through archival releases such as Both Directions at Once: The Lost Album and the expanded Giant Steps anniversary edition. His son Ravi Coltrane, himself a saxophonist, helps steward that legacy. Players from Michael Brecker to Kamasi Washington have built on Coltrane's harmonic and spiritual innovations.
title: John Coltrane
